nameStory: The 'decollate' snail gets its unusual name from a fascinating quirk of growth - as it matures, it deliberately breaks off the tip of its own shell! This process is called decollation, from the Latin meaning 'to behead.' The snail essentially gives itself a controlled haircut, sealing off the broken end with new shell material.
description: The decollate snail is a medium-sized land snail with a distinctive elongated, cone-shaped shell that looks almost like a tiny ice cream cone. Originally from the Mediterranean region, this predatory snail has made its way to various parts of the world, including very rarely to New England. Unlike many garden snails that munch on plants, this one is actually a hunter that preys on other snails and their eggs. Adults typically reach about an inch in length.

idTips.label: Broken shell tip
idTips.description: The most distinctive feature is the deliberately broken-off shell tip, creating a flat or slightly concave opening at the narrow end where you'd expect a pointed spiral

idTips.label: Cone shape
idTips.description: Shell is distinctly cone-shaped or tower-like, much taller than it is wide, resembling a miniature dunce cap rather than the typical rounded snail shell

idTips.label: Shell texture
idTips.description: Shell feels smooth to the touch with a slightly glossy surface, colored in various shades of brown, tan, or yellowish-brown with subtle growth lines

idTips.label: Size and build
idTips.description: Medium-sized at about an inch long, with a relatively sturdy shell that feels substantial when handled, not paper-thin like some smaller snails

habitat: In New England, decollate snails are extremely rare visitors, likely arriving accidentally in plant shipments or garden materials. When found, they prefer areas with loose, well-draining soil such as gardens, compost areas, or disturbed ground near human habitation. They seek shelter under logs, stones, or in leaf litter during the day.

seasonality.spring: Most active as temperatures warm, emerging from winter hiding spots under debris. This is when you're most likely to spot them moving around gardens or disturbed soil areas.
seasonality.summer: Active during humid nights and after rain showers, retreating to cool, moist hiding places during hot, dry days. Look under garden stones or logs in early morning.
seasonality.fall: Continue to be active through early fall, often found near compost piles or areas with decaying organic matter where they hunt for prey.
seasonality.winter: Become dormant in New England's cold, seeking deep shelter under logs, stones, or in protected soil crevices where they remain inactive until spring.

funFact: This snail is nature's pest control specialist - it's been deliberately introduced to some areas because it hunts and eats the eggs of garden pest snails, making it one of the few snails that gardeners actually want around!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with young cone snails or other elongated land snails, but the deliberately broken shell tip is a dead giveaway - no other New England snail intentionally decapitates its own shell like this species does.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'Giant Land Snail' family member, the decollate snail is actually medium-sized - the family name refers to some of its tropical relatives that can grow much larger. In New England, any sighting would be quite remarkable as they're not established here.
compareHints: As the only Rumina species in our region, compare it to other cone-shaped land snails in different families. The decollate snail's broken shell tip and predatory lifestyle set it apart from plant-eating cone snails, and its medium size distinguishes it from tiny needle snails that also have elongated shells.
